chunks.text: A linear equation in n unknowns sets a weighted sum of the unknowns equal to a constant. A system of linear equations can be written compactly as Ax = b, where the matrix A holds the coefficients.
Gaussian elimination reduces a matrix to row echelon form with row swaps, row scalings and row additions. Back substitution then recovers the unknowns one at a time from the last row upward.
The determinant of a square matrix is a single number. It is nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible, and it equals the signed volume scaling of the map the matrix represents.
An eigenvector of a square matrix A is a nonzero vector v that A only stretches: Av = lambda v. The stretch factor lambda is the eigenvalue, found from the roots of the characteristic polynomial.
The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent columns, which always equals the number of independent rows. It measures the dimension of the column space.
The null space of a matrix A contains every vector x with Ax = 0. Its dimension, the nullity, plus the rank equals the number of columns.
Projecting a vector onto a line gives the closest point on that line. The error vector left over is perpendicular to the direction of the line.
When Ax = b has no exact solution, least squares picks the x that minimizes the squared length of the residual Ax - b. That x satisfies the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b.
The singular value decomposition writes any matrix as U Sigma V^T, with orthogonal U and V and nonnegative singular values on the diagonal of Sigma. It works for rectangular matrices too.
The covariance of two random variables measures how they vary together. A positive value means they tend to rise together, and zero means no linear relationship.
Bayes' rule updates a prior probability with evidence: the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. The denominator normalizes the result so that it sums to one.
The central limit theorem says that the average of many independent samples is approximately normally distributed, whatever the shape of the original distribution, as long as its variance is finite.
The gradient of a scalar function points in the direction of steepest increase. Gradient descent takes repeated small steps in the opposite direction to reach a minimum.
The chain rule differentiates a composition of functions: the derivative of f(g(x)) is f'(g(x)) times g'(x). Backpropagation applies it repeatedly through a network.
